newsitem.title: GERMANY: German conservative calls for limits on foreigners.
newsitem.headline: German conservative calls for limits on foreigners.

text.p: Too many immigrants in Germany were taking jobs away from German workers and taxpayers were fed up with the high costs of supporting foreigners, a leading conservative politician was quoted on Saturday as saying.

In unusually blunt language, Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of the Christian Social Union (CSU), said his party would soon propose legislation to tighten restrictions on foreigners coming to Germany and working here.

"We can no longer tolerate the fact that millions of our own citizens are unemployed, but at the same time more than one million foreigners are given work permits in Germany every year," Glos said in an interview to be published in the weekly news magazine Der Spiegel on Monday.
The CSU is the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU). The CSU has long been noted for its arch conservative views.

But German politicians rarely speak out so directly against foreigners, in part because they want to avoid being accused of fomenting racial unrest. They have been especially careful since xenophobic violence erupted in Germany in the early 1990s.
"The 2.7 million foreigners who have arrived since 1988 have overwhelmed the ability of our society to absorb them," Glos said, according to an advance text of the interview released on Saturday.
About nine percent of Germany's population of 81 million are foreign nationals, government data for 1995 shows.
"Politicians need to respond," Glos said. "Taxpayers are no longer willing to pay the high costs for foreign immigrants."
Glos said the CSU will put up the new legislative intiative after the party's annual mid-winter meeting in early January.

At the moment, the proposals are contained in a "six-point-programme" that the CSU leadership will discuss at the party meeting. If it wins endorsement there, the CSU will seek backing for the measures in the Bonn coalition.
The CSU's efforts could run into opposition from its coalition partners, especially the liberal Free Democrats (FDP).
The CSU paper says immigrants "cause considerable social costs" and it aims to "liberate the job market from the pressure of immigrants".

"Social costs for foreigners have tripled since 1990," Glos said. "About 10 percent of all the foreigners living in Germany receive financial support. The number of needy immigrants is constantly increasing. We simply can no longer afford these high costs."
Glos said it was only partially true that foreign immigrants take many of the menial jobs Germans refuse to take because they are considered below their dignity.
He said many foreigners, for example, have taken away good-paying construction jobs from German construction workers, many of whom now are without jobs.

"It is nevertheless true that it is hard to win German workers for many simple jobs -- but that has to end," Glos said. "With four million unemployed, people can not go on thinking they can live at the expense of others because they think they are too good for these jobs."

The one group of immigrants that Glos does not want to see restrictions placed on is the ethnic Germans who since the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe have been moving to Germany from Russia by the thousand.
"The Russian Germans suffered the longest and most under Stalin and the effects of war, just because they were German," he said. "As a result the gate for these people can never be slammed shut."
